sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a partial skeleton featuring a complete skull but missing most hindlimbs, except for the right humerus and left thighbone.
Jinyunpelta possesses two additional openings behind the nostril, known as C1 and C2, which align with the center of the nostril.
The tail club of Jinyunpelta is hexagonal in top view, with its widest point near the rear edge.
Jinyunpelta is the most basal ankylosaur known to possess a proper tail club.
This species is the oldest and most basal ankylosaurid known to possess a tail club, replacing Pinacosaurus as the earliest known holder of this trait.
Jinyunpelta was the southernmost known ankylosaurid in Asia.
A farmer discovered the remains of an ankylosaur at a construction site in Jinyun County, China, in June 2008.
The species Jinyunpelta sinensis was formally named and described in 2018 by a team of six researchers.
The holotype specimen dates to about one hundred million years ago, from the Albian-Cenomanian layers of the Liangtoutang Formation.
Jinyunpelta exhibited biphasal jaw movement, an adaptation previously believed to have evolved later in ankylosaurid history.
In 2018, Jinyunpelta was classified within the subfamily Ankylosaurinae of the family Ankylosauridae.
Jinyunpelta lived approximately 100 to 95 million years ago, during the Albian to Cenomanian stages of the Cretaceous.
The time range for Jinyunpelta is recorded as the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 100.5 million years ago.
